The Roman Empire. From 27 BCE to 476 CE in the West, and 1453 CE in the East as the Byzantine Empire, this was the Western world's longest-lived and most culturally influential empire, lasting over 500 years at its territorial peak. Founded formally when Augustus received the title Imperator in 27 BCE, ending the Republic, Rome at its height under Trajan in 117 CE stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia and controlled the Mediterranean as an inland lake.

The Roman Republic, lasting from 509 to 27 BCE, conquered the Mediterranean through military expansion and the incorporation of conquered peoples as allies or subject states. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul—modern France—and crossed the Rubicon to seize power, triggering civil war. His assassination in 44 BCE destabilized the Republic. Augustus, Caesar's adopted heir, won the civil war and consolidated power by becoming the first Imperator, maintaining republican forms like the Senate and magistrates while wielding absolute authority.

The empire expanded under Augustus and his successors to include Gaul, Spain, North Africa, Egypt, Syria, and Mesopotamia, temporarily under Trajan, who ruled from 98 to 117 CE. Trajan conquered Dacia—modern Romania—and Mesopotamia, bringing the empire to its territorial maximum of roughly 70 million subjects. The Pax Romana, from 27 BCE to 180 CE, was an era of relative internal peace, uninterrupted trade, and cultural flourishing enabled by Roman legions stationed across the empire and Roman law enforcing contract and property.

Rome built a bureaucratic system of provinces with appointed governors, roads, aqueducts, and public buildings—infrastructure that unified the empire and was copied by later empires. Roman law, codified especially under Justinian in the East, established principles of contract, property, citizenship, and due process that influenced Western legal systems for 2,000 years. The empire promoted Latin as the official language and encouraged the spread of Christianity, which eventually became the state religion in 381 CE under Theodosius I, ensuring that Roman cultural influence persisted long after political collapse.

The empire faced increasing pressure from Germanic tribes on the Rhine and Danube frontiers during the third century crisis. Diocletian, ruling from 284 to 305 CE, divided the empire into four regions to govern more effectively. Constantine I, ruling from 306 to 337 CE, moved the capital to Constantinople—modern Istanbul—and legalized Christianity, cementing the eastern empire's continuity. The Byzantine Empire survived until 1453 CE.

The Western Roman Empire fell to Germanic invasions: Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 CE under Alaric, Vandals sacked it again in 455 CE, and the final western emperor Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476 CE. Roman culture—art, literature, law, Christianity, and Latin—became the foundation of Western Europe and influenced the Islamic and Byzantine worlds. The model of empire set the template for all subsequent Western empires.
